nodes.title: Principles of Green Chemistry & Need for Sustainable Chemistry
points: Definition: Green chemistry is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances (Paul T. Anastas, Father of Green Chemistry).
Objective: Sustainable development, resource conservation, minimizing waste, maximizing energy efficiency, and preventing environmental pollution at the molecular level.

The 12 Principles of Green Chemistry (mnemonic: PRODUCTIVELY): 1) Prevention of waste; 2) Atom economy; 3) Less hazardous chemical syntheses; 4) Designing safer chemicals; 5) Safer solvents and auxiliaries; 6) Design for energy efficiency; 7) Use of renewable feedstocks; 8) Reduce derivatives; 9) Catalysis; 10) Design for degradation; 11) Real-time analysis for pollution prevention; 12) Inherently safer chemistry for accident prevention.

formulas.label: Green Chemistry core paradigm
formulas.expr: Source reduction / Prevention > Treatment / Remediation (prevent waste at source)

formulas.label: Father of Green Chemistry
formulas.expr: Paul T. Anastas (formulated the 12 principles of green chemistry)

nodes.title: Atom Economy & Calculation Metrics
points: Principle 2: Atom Economy measures the efficiency of a chemical reaction in terms of all atoms involved and how many end up in the desired product.
Formula: % Atom Economy = [Formula weight of desired product / Total formula weight of all reactants] × 100%.
Addition reactions (e.g. hydrogenation, addition across C=C) have 100% atom economy because all reactant atoms are incorporated into the desired product.
Substitution and elimination reactions have lower atom economy because atoms are lost as side products / waste.
Example: Conversion of butan-1-ol to 1-bromobutane vs Diels-Alder reaction (100% atom economy).

formulas.label: % Atom Economy formula
formulas.expr: % Atom Economy = (Formula weight of desired product / Total formula weight of all reactants) × 100%

formulas.label: 100% atom economy reaction type
formulas.expr: Addition reactions (e.g. CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃-CH₃: 100% atom economy)

formulas.label: Reaction with low atom economy
formulas.expr: Substitution: R-OH + HBr → R-Br + H₂O (water is lost as stoichiometric waste)

nodes.title: Green Syntheses & Safer Alternatives
points: 1. Prevention of waste (Green synthesis of Ibuprofen): Traditional Boots process had 6 steps with only 40% atom economy (60% waste); Green BHC process has 3 catalytic steps with 77% atom economy (up to 99% with recovered acetic acid).

2. Safer Solvents: Replacing hazardous volatile organic compounds (VOCs like benzene, CCl₄, CH₂Cl₂) with Supercritical CO₂ (scCO₂), water (universal green solvent), or ionic liquids (zero vapor pressure).
3. Dry Cleaning of Clothes: Tetrachloroethene (Cl₂C=CCl₂) was traditionally used (carcinogenic, contaminates groundwater); replaced by liquid/supercritical CO₂ with suitable detergent.
4. Bleaching of Paper: Chlorine gas (Cl₂) produces toxic chlorinated dioxins; replaced by Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) in presence of green catalysts.

formulas.label: Green bleaching of pulp reaction
formulas.expr: H₂O₂ (catalyst) → H₂O + [O] (chlorine-free, zero toxic dioxins)

nodes.title: Nanochemistry: The Nanoscale & Definitions
points: Definition: Nanochemistry is the combination of chemistry and nanoscience dealing with the synthesis, characterization, and manipulation of matter at the nanoscale (1 to 100 nanometers).
1 nanometer (nm) = 10⁻⁹ m = 10 Å = 10⁻⁷ cm.
Nanomaterial: Any material having at least one dimension in the nanoscale (1-100 nm).

Why nanoscale is unique: At the nanoscale, materials behave very differently from bulk materials because: 1) Surface area to volume ratio increases exponentially; 2) Quantum confinement effects become dominant (electronic energy levels become discrete instead of continuous bands).

formulas.label: Nanoscale definition range
formulas.expr: 1 nm to 100 nm (at least one spatial dimension)

nodes.title: Classification of Nanomaterials (0D, 1D, 2D, 3D)
points: Classification based on number of dimensions OUTSIDE the nanoscale (or dimensions confined in nanoscale):
1. Zero-Dimensional (0D): All three dimensions are inside nanoscale (<100 nm). No dimensions outside nanoscale (e.g. Nanoparticles, Quantum dots, Nanoclusters).
2. One-Dimensional (1D): Two dimensions are inside nanoscale; one dimension is outside nanoscale (>100 nm) (e.g. Nanowires, Nanorods, Carbon Nanotubes CNTs).
3. Two-Dimensional (2D): One dimension is inside nanoscale; two dimensions are outside nanoscale (>100 nm) (e.g. Graphene, Nanosheets, Nanofilms, Nanolayers).
4. Three-Dimensional (3D): All three dimensions are outside nanoscale (>100 nm), but composed of nanoscale grains/features (e.g. Polycrystalline materials, Nanocomposites, Bundles of CNTs).

formulas.label: 0D Nanomaterials dimension rule
formulas.expr: All 3 dimensions < 100 nm (Quantum dots, Nanoparticles)

formulas.label: 1D Nanomaterials dimension rule
formulas.expr: 2 dimensions < 100 nm, 1 dimension macroscopic (Nanowires, Nanotubes)

formulas.label: 2D Nanomaterials dimension rule
formulas.expr: 1 dimension < 100 nm, 2 dimensions macroscopic (Graphene, Thin films)

formulas.label: 3D Nanomaterials dimension rule
formulas.expr: Bulk composite materials containing nanoscale building blocks

nodes.title: Surface Area to Volume Ratio & Size-Dependent Properties
points: Surface-to-Volume Ratio: For a spherical particle of radius r: S/V = (4πr²) / ((4/3)πr³) = 3/r. As radius decreases, S/V increases drastically! Huge fraction of atoms reside at the surface with unsaturated valencies, making nanoparticles extraordinarily reactive catalysts.

Size-Dependent Properties: 1) Melting Point: Decreases significantly at nanoscale due to large percentage of surface atoms with fewer neighbors. Bulk Gold melts at 1064 °C; 2 nm gold particles melt at ~300 °C!; 2) Optical Properties: Bulk Gold is shiny yellow; Gold nanoparticles (10-20 nm) appear ruby red or purple due to Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR); 3) Electrical Conductivity: Bulk copper is a good conductor; copper nanoparticles under 50 nm lose conductivity due to electron scattering; 4) Mechanical Strength: Carbon Nanotubes (CNTs) are 100 times stronger than steel at 1/6th the weight.

formulas.label: Surface-to-volume ratio of a sphere
formulas.expr: S / V = 3 / r (inversely proportional to radius r)

formulas.label: Surface-to-volume ratio of a cube of edge a
formulas.expr: S / V = (6a²) / a³ = 6 / a

formulas.label: Melting point depression at nanoscale
formulas.expr: T_m(nano) < T_m(bulk) (due to high surface energy and lower cohesive energy)

nodes.title: Synthesis of Nanomaterials: Top-Down vs Bottom-Up
points: 1. Top-Down Approach: Bulk material is broken down, sliced, or milled mechanically into nanoscale particles. Physical methods: Ball milling, High-energy mechanical attrition, Lithography, Etching, Laser ablation. Drawbacks: Imperfection of surface structure, contamination from milling tools, internal stress/defects.

2. Bottom-Up Approach: Building nanomaterials atom-by-atom, molecule-by-molecule, or cluster-by-cluster through chemical condensation. Chemical/biological methods: Sol-gel method, Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD), Hydrothermal synthesis, Colloidal precipitation, Green synthesis using plant extracts. Advantages: Precise control over size, shape, and uniform crystalline structure with minimal defects.

formulas.label: Top-down approach direction
formulas.expr: Bulk material (mechanical milling / laser ablation) → Nanomaterials

formulas.label: Bottom-up approach direction
formulas.expr: Atoms / Molecules (chemical reaction / sol-gel / CVD) → Nanoclusters → Nanomaterials

nodes.title: Characterization Techniques & Applications of Nanotechnology
points: Characterization Techniques: 1) SEM (Scanning Electron Microscopy): Scans surface with focused electron beam; generates 3D-like images of surface topography, morphology, and particle size; 2) TEM (Transmission Electron Microscopy): High-energy electrons pass THROUGH thin specimen; provides ultra-high resolution (atomic scale ~0.1 nm), internal lattice structure, and crystallography; 3) AFM (Atomic Force Microscopy): Mechanical cantilever probe with nanometer tip scans surface; measures interatomic forces to produce 3D surface topography with sub-nanometer resolution; 4) XRD (X-ray Diffraction): Determines crystal structure, phase purity, and crystallite size using Scherrer's equation: D = (0.9λ) / (β cos θ).

Applications: Medicine (targeted drug delivery, MRI contrast agents, cancer hyperthermia); Electronics (CNT transistors, OLED displays); Energy (dye-sensitized solar cells with TiO₂ nanoparticles); Environment (water purification with silver nanoparticles, photocatalytic degradation with nano-TiO₂).

formulas.label: Scherrer formula for crystallite size (XRD)
formulas.expr: D = (K × λ) / (β × cos θ) (where K ≈ 0.9, β = FWHM in radians, λ = X-ray wavelength)

formulas.label: SEM vs TEM electron interaction
formulas.expr: SEM: Backscattered & secondary electrons (surface) | TEM: Transmitted electrons through sample (internal structure)

nodes.title: High-Weightage Board Questions & Principles
points: Board Q1: State any four principles of Green Chemistry with suitable explanations.
Board Q2: Define Atom Economy and calculate % Atom economy for a given chemical reaction.
Board Q3: Differentiate between Top-down and Bottom-up approaches for synthesis of nanomaterials.
Board Q4: Explain why the properties of nanomaterials differ drastically from bulk materials (surface-to-volume ratio and quantum confinement).
Board Q5: Explain the role of supercritical CO₂ as a green solvent in dry cleaning and extraction.

formulas.label: % Atom Economy formula
formulas.expr: % Atom Economy = (Molar mass of desired product / Total molar mass of all reactants) × 100%

formulas.label: 12 Principles mnemonic
formulas.expr: P-R-O-D-U-C-T-I-V-E-L-Y (Prevention, Renewable feedstocks, Optimization, Degradation, Catalysis, etc.)

nodes.title: MHT-CET High-Speed Shortcuts & Dimensionality Traps
points: TRAP 1: Dimensionality classification: 0D = Quantum dots, fullerenes (C₆₀), nanoparticles (all 3 dimensions in nanoscale); 1D = Nanotubes (CNTs), nanowires, nanorods (2 in nano, 1 macroscopic); 2D = Graphene, nanosheets, nanocoatings (1 in nano, 2 macroscopic).
TRAP 2: Ruby red color of gold nanoparticles: Caused by Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR), NOT a chemical reaction! Bulk gold is yellow.
TRAP 3: 100% Atom economy: ALL addition reactions and rearrangement reactions have 100% atom economy. Substitution and elimination reactions NEVER have 100% atom economy.
TRAP 4: Dry cleaning solvent evolution: Benzene → Stoddard solvent → Tetrachloroethene (carcinogen) → Supercritical / Liquid CO₂ with green surfactants.
TRAP 5: Scherrer equation: Particle size D is inversely proportional to peak broadening β (wider XRD peak = smaller nanoparticle crystallite size).

formulas.label: Nanomaterial dimensionality table shortcut
formulas.expr: 0D = 3 dimensions in nanoscale | 1D = 2 in nano, 1 bulk | 2D = 1 in nano, 2 bulk

formulas.label: Scherrer peak broadening relation
formulas.expr: D ∝ 1 / β (broader XRD peak means smaller crystallite size)

formulas.label: Green dry cleaning agent
formulas.expr: Liquid / Supercritical CO₂ + biodegradable surfactant (replaces toxic Cl₂C=CCl₂)
